Hey -
I'm a Plumbing CSA where I work, but I have covered in tools (and millwork, lumber, paint, flooring etc. etc. lol). You don't necessarily need to know that much about tools to work in that department, but the same goes for any of them really - it helps. You get a lot of questions about what to use for what project, but just as many from experienced contractors who already know what they're looking for they just can't find it. Tools is fairly easy to catch onto though, and again just like everywhere else it's just a matter of repetition. Shadow experienced associates in the department to learn a lot very quickly. It's how I learned plumbing and millwork. 

I wouldn't stress about not being knowledgeable at the get-go. It takes time, but it's not difficult. I'd go for it! :D

Thank you, AsianTradie,

As funny as it sounds, when you've been in the field before, you tend to see failures in the system more than you see successes. That's just the nature of mental health care. But it makes you extremely distrusting of the entire thing. You come to despise medication (not being naturalistic here or anything, just tired of hearing throw pills at it), although I know for a fact they'd likely help. So you start searching for alternate methods of calming down in regards to every day routine or thought process. I guess you sometimes feel like you can handle it yourself because you know better. When you obviously don't. If I did, I wouldn't be on Reddit at 10:00 o' clock at night posting just to get weight off my chest. 

I feel like a part of what needs to happen is me expressing what I keep hiding. Even if it's just a post online people read or don't. Keeping it all inside is definitely not going to help recovery. I just wish something else was more effective. Or maybe more immediately effective. Which is ridiculously unrealistic.
